title: How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot REST API using @ControllerAdvice/@RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler, @ResponseStatus, and ResponseStatusException?
shortTitle: @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler — global exception handling in Spring Boot REST

s1_definition.profdef: `@RestControllerAdvice` is a class-level annotation that acts as a GLOBAL exception handler for all controllers. Methods annotated with `@ExceptionHandler(ExceptionType.class)` catch specific exceptions thrown by ANY controller and return a structured error response with proper HTTP status. `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` on a method or exception class sets the HTTP status code. `ResponseStatusException` (Spring 5) is an inline way to throw an exception with a status code: `throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Trade not found")`. The result: ZERO try-catch in controllers — all exceptions propagate to the global handler, which returns consistent error responses across the entire API.
s1_definition.analogy: Instead of every bank teller (controller) having their own error handling procedure (try-catch), the bank has a CENTRAL COMPLAINTS DESK (@ControllerAdvice). ANY complaint from ANY counter goes to this desk. The desk handles each type of complaint (InsufficientFunds → 400, NotFound → 404, ServerError → 500) and gives the customer a standard response form. Tellers just do their job — no error handling needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: @RestControllerAdvice = global exception handler. @ExceptionHandler(X.class) = catch X from ANY controller. @ResponseStatus = HTTP status code. Controllers: ZERO try-catch — all errors go to global handler.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@RestControllerAdvice` is a class-level annotation that acts as a GLOBAL exception handler for all controllers. Methods annotated with `@ExceptionHandler(ExceptionType.class)` catch specific exceptions thrown by ANY controller and return a structured error response with proper HTTP status. `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` on a method or exception class sets the HTTP status code. `ResponseStatusException` (Spring 5) is an inline way to throw an exception with a status code: `throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Trade not found")`. The result: ZERO try-catch in controllers — all exceptions propagate to the global handler, which returns consistent error responses across the entire API.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Instead of every bank teller (controller) having their own error handling procedure (try-catch), the bank has a CENTRAL COMPLAINTS DESK (@ControllerAdvice). ANY complaint from ANY counter goes to this desk. The desk handles each type of complaint (InsufficientFunds → 400, NotFound → 404, ServerError → 500) and gives the customer a standard response form. Tellers just do their job — no error handling needed.

**One line to remember:** @RestControllerAdvice = global exception handler. @ExceptionHandler(X.class) = catch X from ANY controller. @ResponseStatus = HTTP status code. Controllers: ZERO try-catch — all errors go to global handler.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — Every controller had its own try-catch blocks** — 200 try-catch blocks across 15 controllers. Each returned errors in different formats: some JSON, some plain text, some with stack traces. Inconsistent. Maintenance nightmare. Fix: ONE @RestControllerAdvice handles ALL exceptions. Consistent ErrorResponse format. Controllers have ZERO try-catch.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** GET /trades/TRD-999. Controller calls `tradeService.findById("TRD-999")`. Not found → throws `TradeNotFoundException`.

**Step 2.** Exception propagates out of controller. Spring's DispatcherServlet routes it to @RestControllerAdvice.

**Step 3.** GlobalExceptionHandler matches `@ExceptionHandler(TradeNotFoundException.class)`. Executes the handler method. Returns `ErrorResponse("NOT_FOUND", "Trade not found: TRD-999", 404)`.

**Step 4.** `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)` sets HTTP 404. Spring serializes ErrorResponse to JSON. Client receives structured error.

**Step 5.** Controller had ZERO try-catch. Service just throws. Handler handles. Clean separation.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ GLOBAL EXCEPTION HANDLING FLOW ═══

  Client → Controller → Service → throws exception
                ↓
  DispatcherServlet catches unhandled exception
                ↓
  @RestControllerAdvice (GlobalExceptionHandler)
    ├─ @ExceptionHandler(TradeNotFoundException.class)  → 404
    ├─ @ExceptionHandler(InsufficientBalanceException.class) → 400
    ├─ @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class) → 400
    └─ @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) → 500 (catch-all)
                ↓
  ErrorResponse JSON → Client

  ═══ BEFORE (200 try-catch blocks) ═══
  Each controller: try { } catch (X) { return error; }
  Inconsistent formats. Duplicated code. Maintenance hell.

  ═══ AFTER (ONE @RestControllerAdvice) ═══
  Controllers: ZERO try-catch. Just call service.
  One handler class: consistent format. One place to maintain.
```

```
       │ throws

  Spring DispatcherServlet

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` methods is the Spring Boot standard for global exception handling. Each @ExceptionHandler catches a specific exception type from ANY controller and returns a structured error response with proper HTTP status. The controller has ZERO try-catch blocks — it just calls the service. If the service throws, the exception propagates to the global handler. `@ResponseStatus` sets the HTTP code (404, 400, 500). `ResponseStatusException` is an inline alternative for simple cases: `throw new ResponseStatusException(NOT_FOUND, "Trade not found")`.

In my banking API, the global handler maps: TradeNotFoundException → 404, InsufficientBalanceException → 400, IllegalArgumentException → 400, and Exception (catch-all) → 500. Every response uses the same ErrorResponse format: `{error, message, status, timestamp}`. Before: 200 try-catch blocks across 15 controllers with inconsistent error formats. After: ONE handler class, consistent responses, controllers have zero error-handling code.

Best practices: order handlers from MOST SPECIFIC to LEAST SPECIFIC (TradeNotFoundException before Exception). Log the full stack trace in the catch-all handler. NEVER expose internal details (SQL errors, stack traces) to the client — return generic "Something went wrong" for 500s. Include a request correlation ID in the ErrorResponse for tracing. Use Problem Details (RFC 7807) format for standards-compliant error responses.
